ta-l1d22q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus opening Lombard's treatment of the names that signify the unity of essence and the plurality of persons (Distinctions 22–25), after the treatment of essence and persons themselves. He first divides the divine names to show what is predicated plurally and singularly of the persons, and then (Dist. 24) how unity and plurality are understood in God. Within the first part he gives a general division of divine names and then (Dist. 23) treats the special difficulty of 'person', which seems not to follow the pattern of the others. The general division is threefold, after Ambrose and Augustine, to which Lombard adds three further modes, including names said of God from time, making six differences, and rules for how each kind is predicated. Four articles are announced: whether God is nameable, whether any name is said of him properly or all metaphorically, whether he should be named by one name, several, or all, and the multiplication of divine names in the text.
claims: The divine names are divided threefold (after Ambrose and Augustine), with further differences added by Lombard.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e121.summary: First argument that God is not nameable. Dionysius says God is incomprehensible to all, and there is no sense, image, opinion, name, word, touch, or knowledge of him. The Liber de causis says the first cause is above description and tongues fail to describe it.
claims: God is above every name and description.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e130.summary: Second argument. Every name is a sign of some form existing in the soul (the Philosopher), but God, who escapes every form, cannot be penetrated by the intellect (Augustine).
claims: God escapes every form.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e133.summary: Third argument. If God is named, it is by noun, pronoun, verb, or participle. Not by a noun, since every noun signifies substance with quality, and in God there is no composition of substance and quality. Not by verb or participle, which co-signify time. Not by pronoun, since a pronoun's signification is determined by pointing or by relation: pointing works through accidents, which God lacks, and relation recalls something already named.
claims: No part of speech fits God.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e137.summary: Sed contra from Psalm 67:5 ('the Lord is his name') and Exodus 3 ('if they ask my name').
claims: Scripture gives God names.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e146.summary: Second sed contra. Whatever is known can be signified by speech, and we know God in some way, by faith or by natural knowledge.
claims: What is known can be named.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e149.summary: Thomas's determination. Since words are signs of concepts (the Philosopher), the judgment about knowing a thing and naming it is the same. As we know God imperfectly, we name him imperfectly, as if stammering (Gregory). Only God comprehends himself, and so only he names himself perfectly, so to speak, by begetting the Word equal to himself.
claims: We name God as we know him, imperfectly, as if stammering.
God alone names himself perfectly, in begetting the Word.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e152.summary: Reply to the first argument. All the authorities saying God is unnameable mean that no name perfectly expresses God, as the Philosopher's words show: tongues fail to describe him, and the first cause is above all description and above everything that is named.
claims: God is called unnameable because no name expresses him perfectly.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e161.summary: Reply to the second argument. If Augustine means bodily form, God plainly has none, and not everything named must have bodily form. If he means form absolutely, God escapes every form not because he is not truly form, being pure act, simple and first form (Boethius), but because whatever form the intellect conceives, God escapes it by his eminence: if our intellect grasps wisdom, God in his wisdom exceeds every wisdom we understand. So he is not penetrable by our intellect so that it could reach him by comprehending him. Hence Dionysius says that whatever we affirm of God can also be denied of him, because it does not belong to him as we understand and signify it, but more excellently.
claims: God is the first form but exceeds every form the intellect conceives.
Whatever is affirmed of God can be denied as we understand it.
concepts: God as pure act and first form

ta-l1d22q1-d1e164.summary: Reply to the third argument. God can be signified by noun, pronoun, verb, and participle. 'A noun signifies substance with quality' does not take substance and quality as the logician does in distinguishing the categories. The grammarian takes substance as a mode of signifying: what a noun signifies is signified as something subsistent of which something can be predicated, even if it is not subsistent in reality, as 'whiteness' signifies a substance in this sense, unlike a verb. In every noun one also considers that from which it is imposed, the principle by which the thing is made known, and this has the mode of quality, since quality or form is the principle of knowing a thing; the Philosopher even calls substantial form a quality in one sense. It makes no difference whether the principle of knowing is really the same as what the noun signifies, as in abstract names, or different, as in 'man'. Since God is known through himself, he can be signified by a noun having quality in the concept from which it is imposed and substance in what it is imposed to signify. He can be signified by a pronoun ('I am who am', Exod. 3:14), pointed out not to sense but to intellect according to what it grasps of him, and by a relative pronoun referring to a noun that names him. He can be signified by verbs and participles ('he is understanding, powerful'), which do not signify anything temporal in him, though in their mode of signifying time they fall short of representing him.
claims: God can be signified by every part of speech, since grammatical 'substance' and 'quality' are modes of signifying, not categories.
The temporal mode of verbs falls short of God without falsifying what they signify.
concepts: naming God by pronouns and verbs

ta-l1d22q1-d1e179.summary: First argument that no name is said of God properly. Nothing is said properly of something that is more truly denied than affirmed of it, and according to Dionysius every name said of God is more truly denied than affirmed, so negations in God are true and affirmations are 'unfitted'.
claims: Divine names are more truly denied than affirmed.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e182.summary: Second argument. We can name God only as we know him, only from his effects, by causality, negation, or eminence. So we name him only from creatures, and whenever a creature's name is predicated of God the predication is true only metaphorically ('God is a lion', 'God is a stone').
claims: We name God only from creatures, which seems to make all names metaphorical.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e185.summary: Third argument. Created wisdom or being differs more from God than a meadow's flowering from human laughter, and a meadow is said to laugh only metaphorically.
claims: The distance between creature and God exceeds that between meadow and laughter.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e189.summary: Fourth argument. A name implying a bodily condition contrary to God's dignity is said of him only metaphorically, and every name we impose implies some condition contrary to divine dignity: verbs co-signify time, abstract names signify something imperfect and non-subsistent, concrete names imply composition.
claims: Every name we impose implies some unfitting condition.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e192.summary: Sed contra. What is said of things by priority and posteriority belongs more properly to that of which it is said first, as being belongs first to substance. Some names are said first of God, like paternity ('from whom all paternity in heaven and on earth is named', Eph. 3:15), and likewise goodness and the like.
claims: Some names are said first of God.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e198.summary: Second sed contra. Dionysius distinguishes symbolic names, said metaphorically, from other divine names, so not all are said by transference, as the division of Augustine and Ambrose in the text also shows.
claims: Dionysius distinguishes symbolic from proper names.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e201.summary: Thomas's determination. Although every perfection in creatures descends exemplarily from God, the principle who contains all perfections in a unified way, no creature can receive that perfection in the way it is in God, so by its mode of receiving it falls short of perfectly representing its exemplar, and there are grades among creatures, some participating more and nobler perfections. So in names two things are to be considered: the thing signified and the mode of signifying. Since we impose names knowing God only from creatures, they always fall short of representing God as to mode of signifying, signifying divine perfections as participated in creatures. As to the thing signified, some names are imposed to signify principally the perfection modelled on God simply, without involving any mode in their signification; others to signify the perfection as received in a particular mode of participation. All cognition is modelled on divine cognition and all science on divine science, but 'sense' signifies cognition in the mode in which it is received materially by a power joined to an organ, while 'cognition' signifies no mode of participation in its principal meaning. So names imposed to signify a perfection absolutely, such as wisdom, goodness, essence, are said properly of God and belong to him first as to the thing signified, though not as to the mode of signifying; these are what Anselm calls simply and wholly better to be than not to be. Names imposed to signify a perfection modelled on God that include an imperfect mode of participation in their signification are in no way said properly of God, though by reason of that perfection they can be said of him metaphorically, such as sensing and seeing, and likewise all bodily forms, stone, lion, and the like, which signify bodily forms in a determinate mode of participating being, life, or some divine perfection.
claims: In names one must distinguish the thing signified from the mode of signifying.
Names signifying perfection absolutely (wisdom, goodness) are said properly and first of God as to the thing signified.
Names whose signification includes an imperfect mode of participation (sense, lion) are said of God only metaphorically.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e204.summary: Reply to the first argument. Since a name has a mode of signifying and a thing signified, it can always be removed from God in one or both respects, but can be said of God only in one, the thing signified. The truth and propriety of an affirmation require that the whole be affirmed, while for a negation it suffices that one part be lacking. So Dionysius says negations are absolutely true and affirmations only in a qualified way, as to the thing signified and not the mode of signifying.
claims: Negations of divine names are absolutely true; affirmations are true as to the thing signified, not the mode.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e207.summary: Reply to the second argument. Although we name God only from creatures, we do not always name him from a perfection proper to creatures in their mode of participating it. We can impose a name on the perfection itself absolutely, without involving any mode in the thing signified, which is like the intellect's object, though in what is co-signified the creature's mode must always be taken on the side of the intellect, which naturally takes its mode of understanding from sensible things. Such names are said properly of God.
claims: Names can signify a perfection absolutely while co-signifying the creaturely mode of understanding.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e211.summary: Reply to the third argument. Created wisdom differs more from uncreated wisdom in being, which lies in the mode of having, than a meadow's flowering from human laughter. But as to the concept from which the name is imposed they agree more, since that concept is one by analogy, existing first in God and secondarily in creatures, and the truth and propriety of a locution depend more on the concept signified than on the mode of signifying, which is understood consequently.
claims: Created and uncreated wisdom share one analogical concept, though they differ more in being.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e214.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. When a bodily condition is implied by the principal signification, the name can be said of God only metaphorically. But an imperfection in the mode of signifying that does not fit God makes the predication not false or improper but imperfect, which is why no name perfectly represents God.
claims: Imperfection in the mode of signifying makes divine predication imperfect, not improper.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e226.summary: First argument that God has only one name. A name should correspond to what it signifies, since speech is subject to the thing (Hilary), and in God there is supreme unity without diversity.
claims: Speech is subject to the thing.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e229.summary: Second argument. There are only two modes of predication in God, by substance and by relation, and names differ only by what they signify or by mode of signifying, so there should be one name for the unity of the thing, or at most two for the two modes.
claims: Only two modes of predication exist in God.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e232.summary: Anticipates the reply that divine names are multiplied by being taken from different creatures. God is the efficient and exemplar principle of every creature, so if divine names were multiplied by the diversity of creatures, the names of all creatures could be said of him, which is false.
claims: God's names would include all creatures' names.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e236.summary: Anticipates the reply that they are multiplied only conceptually. A conceptual diversity is a diversity in the intellect, and a diversity in the intellect imposing names, with no diversity in the thing, multiplies names only as synonyms multiply. Then all divine names would be synonyms, which the Commentator expressly denies (Metaphysics 11): 'living' and 'life' are not synonyms in God, much less 'living' and 'wise'.
claims: Merely conceptual diversity would make divine names synonyms.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e239.summary: Sed contra. Scripture contains many names of God.
claims: Scripture gives many divine names.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e242.summary: Second sed contra. No name suffices to express divine perfection, and one name conveys something of perfection another does not, so we should name him by many names to make his perfection better known.
claims: Many names convey more of divine perfection.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e245.summary: Thomas's determination. Names can be multiplied in two ways. On the side of the intellect: since names express concepts, one and the same thing can be signified by different names as it is grasped differently. So we name God as he is in himself and as he relates to creatures, either by negations removing creaturely conditions, which yields negative names multiplied by the conditions denied, especially those common to all creatures (immense, uncreated), or by a relation of God to creatures, which is really in the creature and not in God, yielding names like Lord and King. On the side of the thing, names signify what is in God. In God there is no real distinction except of the persons, three things, from which come the many personal names. Besides this there is a distinction of concepts that are really and truly in God, the concepts of wisdom, goodness, and the like, which are really one and differ conceptually in a way preserved in the propriety and truth of the thing, as God is truly wise and good, not only in the reasoner's intellect. From these come the various names of attributes, which signify one thing but not by one concept, so they are not synonyms.
claims: Divine names multiply by our ways of grasping God (negations, relations to creatures) and by what is in God (persons, attributes).
Attribute names signify one thing by different concepts truly founded in God, so they are not synonyms.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e248.summary: Reply to the first argument. Although there is unity in the essential reality, there is plurality in the personal reality, in the concepts by which the one essence can be signified differently, and in the intellect's different ways of grasping, by all of which divine names are multiplied.
claims: Divine names multiply by persons, concepts, and modes of apprehension.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e251.summary: Reply to the second argument. Equivocal, analogical, and univocal terms are divided differently: the equivocal by the things signified, the univocal by differences, and the analogical by different modes. Being, predicated analogically of the ten categories, is divided into them by different modes, so each category has its proper mode of predication. Since in God only two genera are preserved by the common character of genus, substance and relation, there are two modes of predication in God. Each genus is divided univocally into its species, so species do not have a proper mode of predication. So although some things in the category of quality are said of God by the concept of the species, they bring no new mode of predication, though they bring a new concept of signifying. Hence, though God has only two modes of predication, there are many concepts of signifying by which divine names can be multiplied.
claims: God has two modes of predication (substance, relation) but many concepts of signifying.
Analogical terms divide by modes, univocal by differences, equivocal by things signified.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e255.summary: Reply to the third argument. Some names are said of God properly and belong to him first as to what they signify (goodness, wisdom), and their diversity is not taken from relation to creatures but the reverse: because the concepts of wisdom and goodness differ in God, goodness and wisdom differ in creatures not only conceptually but really, though the diversity of these names as predicated of God becomes known to us from their diversity in creatures. Other names are said of him by transference and multiply according to the creatures whose names are transferred to God. Not every creature's name need be applied, since some imply deformity and defect of which God is not the author, especially the defect of sin, so we cannot call God sinner or devil (the name of a depraved nature), though by transference he is called lion, lamb, or even angry.
claims: Proper names' diversity in God is the cause of the diversity of perfections in creatures, not the reverse.
Metaphorical names multiply by creatures, excluding names of defect and sin.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e258.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The names of attributes differ conceptually, but by a concept not only in the reasoner but preserved in the thing according to its truth and propriety. All these are said of God and creatures not equivocally but by one analogical concept, so since in creatures the concept of wisdom is not that of goodness, this must also be true in God. The difference is that in God they are really the same, while in creatures they differ really and not only conceptually.
claims: Attribute concepts are one analogically in God and creatures, so their conceptual distinctness holds in God.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e271.summary: First argument that Ambrose's division is insufficient. 'Trinity' and 'person' are divine names that pertain neither to the unity of majesty, nor properly to any one person, nor are said by transference.
claims: 'Trinity' and 'person' fit none of Ambrose's three members.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e274.summary: Second argument. Some names are said of God negatively (uncreated, immense), which predicate nothing and so pertain neither to the persons' properties nor to the majesty of deity, nor are they said by transference, since they do not belong to creatures.
claims: Negative names fit none of Ambrose's members.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e277.summary: Third argument. The majesty of deity and personal properties are eternal, but some names are said of God from time, like Lord, which belong to neither and are not said by transference.
claims: Temporal names fit none of Ambrose's members.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e281.summary: Fourth point, presenting Damascene's division: some names signify the infinite ocean of substance and not what it is ('He who is'); some name an operation ('God'); some signify what follows substance ('just', 'good'); some a relation to what God is distinguished from, creatures; and some what he is not ('incorporeal', 'immense').
claims: Damascene gives a fivefold division of divine names.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e284.summary: Fifth point. Dionysius gives a manifold division of divine names, and Lombard adds three differences to Ambrose's threefold division, making six, so the assignment of these divisions is questioned.
claims: Several divisions of divine names must be reconciled.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e287.summary: Thomas's determination. The first, threefold division in the text sufficiently covers all divine names and belongs to Augustine, Ambrose, and Dionysius. Dionysius divides divine names into those said by transference, which he calls symbolic theology, and those said properly, which are first in God, and divides the latter into unified theology, concerning what is predicated of the three persons in common, and distinct theology, concerning what pertains to each person. Its sufficiency is evident: God is named either by what is first in him and secondarily in creatures, or by a likeness taken from creatures. The second gives names said by transference. The first is twofold: what is first in God is either common, pertaining to the unity of majesty, or proper to a person, pertaining to the distinction of the Trinity.
claims: The threefold division (metaphorical, common-proper, personal-proper) sufficiently covers all divine names.
It corresponds to Dionysius's symbolic, unified, and distinct theology.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e290.summary: Reply to the first argument. 'Trinity', though it does not explicitly name what is proper to any person, implicitly includes all the persons' properties, being a kind of collective of the persons. 'Person', though not imposed from a special personal property, is imposed from personality, which signifies property in common and in a way also signifies substance (Dist. 26).
claims: 'Trinity' collects the personal properties; 'person' signifies personality in common.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e293.summary: Reply to the second argument. Every negation is caused by some affirmation, so in God the concept of negative names is founded on that of affirmative ones, as 'incorporeal' is founded on being simple. So negative names reduce to the unity of essence (uncreated, immense) or to the distinction of persons (unbegotten).
claims: Negative names are founded on affirmative ones and reduce to essence or persons.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e296.summary: Reply to the third argument. Although these names posit nothing temporal in God, since the temporal relations are really in creatures and only conceptually in God, as arising from God's operations on creatures they give one to understand something absolutely in God, as the relation of lordship implies the power by which he governs all creatures. So these names also reduce to those pertaining to the unity of majesty (Creator, Lord) or to the distinction of persons (sent, incarnate).
claims: Temporal names imply something absolute in God and reduce to essential or personal names.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e300.summary: Reply to the remaining points. Damascene's division concerns only one member of the threefold division, since all it lists pertain to the unity of majesty. That unity can be named by what is in God or by the intellect's comparison of him to creatures. As to what is in him, there are three kinds of names corresponding to essence, power, and operation, really one and conceptually distinct in God: 'He who is' from essence, 'just' and 'wise' (following the substance) from power, and 'God' from operation. As to comparison with creatures, there are negative names, removing creaturely features, and names implying a causal relation to creatures, whose conditions are removed from God. Dionysius's division is the same as Ambrose's, except that he multiplies the names pertaining to the unity of majesty according to the various processions found in creatures (good, wise, existing). Lombard's three added differences specify Ambrose's division by special modes and reduce to it: among personal names, some name a person's proper feature (Father, Son) and some collect them (Trinity); among both essential and personal names, some belong to God from eternity and some from time, and of the latter some are relative by name (Lord) and some not (incarnate). So Lombard's additions are contained in Ambrose's division by reduction, though not simply.
claims: Damascene's division subdivides essential names by essence, power, and operation, and by negation and causal relation.
Dionysius's and Lombard's divisions reduce to Ambrose's threefold one.

ta-l1d22q1-d1e309.summary: An expositio textus. (1) It seems the treatment of names does not belong to theology, since one science does not consider things and names. But theology, as the principal of all sciences, has something of all the sciences in it and treats not only things but the signification of names, since salvation requires not only faith in the truth of things but vocal confession through names ('with the heart one believes unto justice, with the mouth confession is made unto salvation', Rom. 10:10). (2) Listing 'splendour' among metaphorical names seems wrong, since light is said more properly of spiritual than of bodily things (Augustine). As to the thing signified, light is properly in bodies and said of spiritual things only metaphorically, but as to the concept from which the name is imposed, manifestation, it is more properly in spiritual things (Book II, Dist. 13). (3) 'Incarnate' and 'humanized' are not relative by name, though they implicitly include a relation, since they include union in their concept. (4) Lombard's rules: essential names are said absolutely, signify substance, are said of each person, and are said of all in the singular; personal names are said relatively, do not predicate the divine substance, and are not said of all persons. 'Lord', though relative, pertains to the unity of essence, because the relation is only conceptual in God (Dist. 30). Relations are really the divine essence but not conceptually, and since they are preserved in God by the character of their genus they keep the special mode of predication of that genus, while goodness and wisdom, though conceptually different from the essence, are predicated substantially because the generic character that determines the mode of predication is not preserved in God. 'Not three great ones but one great one' holds if 'great' is substantival, while adjectivally it can be plural, taking number from supposits. (5) Augustine's proof that God is great substantially: what is not great substantially is great by participating a magnitude that is not its substance, and the magnitude participated is greater than what is great by it, so something is greater than anything not great substantially, and nothing is greater than God. Against the objection that the concrete is not predicated of the abstract and that participated magnitude is no less than its participant, Thomas explains that Augustine argues generally of all names signifying accidents in other things and assumes that the abstract is predicated more than the concrete: that is greater which more truly has the concept of magnitude, and predication by essence is always more principal than by participation. Whiteness is more truly white than a white thing, though not in the same way, since what is in the effect is in the cause more eminently, as Dionysius says the cause is life or light and the effect living or illumined.
claims: Theology treats names as well as things, since salvation requires confession by names.
'Light' is properly bodily in its thing signified but more properly spiritual in its ratio of manifestation.
Relations keep their generic mode of predication in God, while attributes are predicated substantially.
Predication by essence is more principal than by participation, so God is great substantially.

ta-l1d22q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 22 opens Lombard's treatment of the divine names signifying unity of essence and plurality of persons. It notes his threefold division after Ambrose and Augustine, his three added differences and rules, and the special case of 'person', and announces four articles.

ta-l1d22q1-Dd1e113.summary: Article 1 asks whether God is nameable. Since naming follows knowing, we name God imperfectly, as if stammering, as we know him imperfectly, and only God names himself perfectly, in begetting the Word. Authorities calling God unnameable mean no name expresses him perfectly. God is the first form but exceeds every concept, so whatever is affirmed of him can be denied as we understand it. Grammatical 'substance' and 'quality' are modes of signifying, so God can be named by noun, pronoun, verb, and participle.
claims: God is nameable imperfectly, as he is known.
God alone names himself perfectly in the Word.

ta-l1d22q1-Dd1e171.summary: Article 2 asks whether any name is said properly of God. Thomas distinguishes the thing signified from the mode of signifying. All names fall short of God in their mode, signifying perfections as participated in creatures. Names imposed to signify a perfection absolutely (wisdom, goodness, being) are said properly and first of God as to the thing signified, while names whose signification includes an imperfect mode of participation (sense, lion) are said only metaphorically. Hence negations are absolutely true and affirmations true as to the thing signified. Created and uncreated wisdom share one analogical concept, and imperfection in the mode of signifying makes predication imperfect, not improper.
claims: Names of pure perfections are said properly and first of God as to the thing signified.
Names including a creaturely mode of participation are said of God only metaphorically.

ta-l1d22q1-Dd1e218.summary: Article 3 asks whether God has one name or many. Divine names multiply on the side of the intellect, as negative names and names of relation to creatures, and on the side of the thing, as personal names for the really distinct persons and as attribute names for concepts really founded in God. Attribute names signify one thing by different concepts and so are not synonyms. God has only two modes of predication, substance and relation, but many concepts of signifying. The diversity of proper names in God causes rather than follows the diversity of perfections in creatures, and metaphorical names exclude names of defect and sin.
claims: Divine names multiply by persons, attribute concepts, negations, and relations to creatures.
Attribute names are not synonyms, since their concepts are truly founded in God.

ta-l1d22q1-Dd1e263.summary: Article 4 examines the divisions of divine names. Thomas holds that the threefold division, into metaphorical names, proper names common to the persons, and proper names of the persons (Dionysius's symbolic, unified, and distinct theology), suffices. 'Trinity' and 'person', negative names, and temporal names all reduce to it. Damascene's division subdivides the essential names by essence, power, and operation and by negation and causal relation, and Dionysius's and Lombard's further divisions reduce to Ambrose's.
claims: The threefold division of divine names is sufficient; other divisions reduce to it.

ta-l1d22q1-Dd1e304.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 22 justifies theology's treatment of names by the necessity of confession and explains 'light' as metaphorical in its thing signified but more proper in spiritual things in its concept. It sets out Lombard's rules for essential and personal names, explains why relations keep their generic mode of predication, and interprets Augustine's argument that God is great substantially because predication by essence is more principal than by participation.
claims: Theology treats names because salvation requires confession.
Predication by essence is more principal than by participation.

ta-l1d22q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 22 gives Thomas's general theory of divine names. Article 1 holds that God is nameable as he is known, imperfectly, and that he names himself perfectly only in the Word. Article 2 distinguishes the thing signified from the mode of signifying. Names of pure perfections are said properly and first of God as to the thing signified, while names whose meaning includes a creaturely mode are said only metaphorically, so negations are absolutely true and affirmations true as to the thing signified. Article 3 explains the multiplicity of divine names by the persons, by attribute concepts truly founded in God, which makes them non-synonymous, and by negations and relations to creatures, within only two modes of predication. Article 4 holds that the threefold division of names, metaphorical, common-proper, and personal-proper, is sufficient and reconciles the divisions of Damascene, Dionysius, and Lombard. The Expositio justifies theology's concern with names and treats Lombard's rules of divine predication.
claims: God is named imperfectly, as known; he names himself perfectly in the Word.
Names of pure perfections are said properly of God as to the thing signified, though not as to the mode of signifying.
Divine names are many and non-synonymous, founded on the persons and on truly distinct concepts in God.
The threefold division of divine names is sufficient.
